Yesterday we learned that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit alleging that Apple Photos' facial recognition feature violates state privacy laws to proceed.

Despite the two companies having very different approaches to privacy, this case has long been conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition. The judge fundamentally misunderstood how the feature works in allowing the case to proceed...

On the earlier allegations against Meta

To understand this properly, we need to start with a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta dating back to 2015.

Since that facial recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify those faces, the company actually broke the law and the case had merit, eventually settling for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which prohibits companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is completely different

There's a major problem with this allegation: when Apple performs facial recognition in the Apple Photos app, it absolutely does not collect biometric data. As Apple explained in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Furthermore, all the iPhone does is tell you "these photos look like they might be the same person" — it doesn't actually know who that person is. Only the iPhone user themselves can attach a name to those faces.

Apple Photos' privacy policy reflects this as well.

I'm stunned that this lawsuit has been allowed to languish in the justice system for six years; just a few minutes of research would have revealed that the lawsuit's allegations are clearly wrong.

Courts and legislators should be applauding Apple for this privacy-preserving approach, rather than conflating it with privacy-violating practices from companies like Meta.

This further illustrates that courts and legislators fundamentally don't understand the technology they're trying to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, involves end-to-end encryption — multiple countries have threatened or tried to ban end-to-end encryption without understanding how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians can't be experts in every area they need to deal with. But they have access to experts, and I'm staggered that these lawsuits and draft bills have been able to progress this far without someone pointing out these fundamental flaws.
